verses.zh: 在安提阿的教会中，有几位先知和教师，就是巴拿巴和称呼尼结的西面、古利奈人路求，与分封之王希律同养的马念，并扫罗。
verses.en: Now there were these prophets and teachers in the church at Antioch:[NOTE:1] Barnabas, Simeon called Niger,[NOTE:2] Lucius the Cyrenian,[NOTE:3] Manaen (a close friend of Herod[NOTE:4] the tetrarch[NOTE:5] from childhood[NOTE:6]) and Saul.
notes: Antioch was a city in Syria (not Antioch in Pisidia).map For location see JP1-F2; JP2-F2; JP3-F2; JP4-F2.
Simeon may well have been from North Africa, since the Latin loanword Niger refers to someone as “dark-complexioned.”
The Cyrenian refers to a native of the city of Cyrene, on the coast of northern Africa west of Egypt.
Herod is generally taken as a reference to Herod Antipas, who governed Galilee from 4 b.c. to a.d. 39, who had John the Baptist beheaded, and who is mentioned a number of times in the gospels.

Or “the governor.”sn A tetrarch was a ruler with rank and authority lower than a king, who ruled only with the approval of the Roman authorities. This was roughly equivalent to being governor of a region. Several times in the NT, Herod tetrarch of Galilee is called a king (Matt 14:9, Mark 6:14-29), reflecting popular usage.

Or “(a foster brother of Herod the tetrarch).” The meaning “close friend from childhood” is given by L&N 34.15, but the word can also mean “foster brother” (L&N 10.51). BDAG 976 s.v. σύντροφας states, “pert. to being brought up with someone, either as a foster-brother or as a companion/friend,” which covers both alternatives. Context does not given enough information to be certain which is the case here, although many modern translations prefer the meaning “close friend from childhood.”

verses.zh: 他们事奉主、禁食的时候，圣灵说：「要为我分派巴拿巴和扫罗，去做我召他们所做的工。」
verses.en: While they were serving[NOTE:1] the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart[NOTE:2] for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.”
notes: This term is frequently used in the LXX of the service performed by priests and Levites in the tabernacle (Exod 28:35, 43; 29:30; 30:20; 35:19; 39:26; Num 1:50; 3:6, 31) and the temple (2 Chr 31:2; 35:3; Joel 1:9, 13; 2:17, and many more examples). According to BDAG 591 s.v. λειτουργέω 1.b it is used “of other expression of religious devotion.” Since the previous verse described the prophets and teachers in the church at Antioch, it is probable that the term here describes two of them (Barnabas and Saul) as they were serving in that capacity. Since they were not in Jerusalem where the temple was located, general religious service is referred to here.
Or “Appoint.”

verses.zh: 于是禁食祷告，按手在他们头上，就打发他们去了。
verses.en: Then, after they had fasted[NOTE:1] and[NOTE:2] prayed and placed their hands[NOTE:3] on them, they sent them off.
notes: The three aorist participles νηστεύσαντες (nēsteusantes), προσευξάμενοι (proseuxamenoi), and ἐπιθέντες (epithentes) are translated as temporal participles. Although they could indicate contemporaneous time when used with an aorist main verb, logically here they are antecedent. On fasting and prayer, see Matt 6:5, 16; Luke 2:37; 5:33; Acts 14:23.

Normally English style, which uses a coordinating conjunction between only the last two elements of a series of three or more, would call for omission of “and” here. However, since the terms “fasting and prayer” are something of a unit, often linked together, the conjunction has been retained here.
The placing of hands on Barnabas and Saul (traditionally known as “the laying on of hands”) refers to an act picturing the commission of God and the church for the task at hand.

verses.zh: 他们既被圣灵差遣，就下到西流基，从那里坐船往塞浦路斯去。
verses.en: So Barnabas and Saul,[NOTE:1] sent out by the Holy Spirit, went down to Seleucia,[NOTE:2] and from there they sailed to Cyprus.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “they”; the referents (Barnabas and Saul) have been specified in the translation for clarity.
Seleucia was the port city of Antioch in Syria.
Cyprus was a large island in the Mediterranean off the south coast of Asia Minor.

verses.zh: 到了撒拉米，就在犹太人各会堂里传讲　神的道，也有约翰作他们的帮手。
verses.en: When[NOTE:1] they arrived[NOTE:2] in Salamis,[NOTE:3] they began to proclaim[NOTE:4] the word of God in the Jewish synagogues.[NOTE:5] (Now they also had John[NOTE:6] as their assistant.)[NOTE:7]
notes: Grk “And when.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.
The participle γενόμενοι (genomenoi) is taken temporally.
Salamis was a city on the southeastern coast of the island of Cyprus. This was a commercial center and a center of Judaism.
The imperfect verb κατήγγελλον (katēngellon) has been translated as an ingressive imperfect.
See the note on synagogue in 6:9.
John refers here to John Mark (see Acts 12:25).

This is a parenthetical note by the author.tn The word ὑπηρέτης (hupēretēs) usually has the meaning “servant,” but it is doubtful John Mark fulfilled that capacity for Barnabas and Saul. He was more likely an apprentice or assistant to them.

verses.zh: 经过全岛，直到帕弗，在那里遇见一个有法术、假充先知的犹太人，名叫巴•耶稣。
verses.en: When they had crossed over[NOTE:1] the whole island as far as Paphos,[NOTE:2] they found a magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus,[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “had passed through,” “had traveled through.”
Paphos. A city on the southwestern coast of the island of Cyprus. It was the seat of the Roman proconsul.

Named Bar-Jesus. “Jesus” is the Latin form of the name “Joshua.” The Aramaic “bar” means “son of,” so this man was surnamed “son of Joshua.” The scene depicts the conflict between Judaism and the emerging new faith at a cosmic level, much like the Simon Magus incident in Acts 8:9-24. Paul’s ministry looks like Philip’s and Peter’s here.

verses.zh: 这人常和方伯士求•保罗同在。士求•保罗是个通达人，他请了巴拿巴和扫罗来，要听　神的道。
verses.en: who was with the proconsul[NOTE:1] Sergius Paulus, an intelligent man. The proconsul[NOTE:2] summoned[NOTE:3] Barnabas and Saul and wanted to hear[NOTE:4] the word of God.
notes: The proconsul was the Roman official who ruled over a province traditionally under the control of the Roman senate.
Grk “This one”; the referent (the proconsul) is specified in the translation for clarity.
Grk “summoning Barnabas and Saul, wanted to hear.” The participle προσκαλεσάμενος (proskalesamenos) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.
The proconsul…wanted to hear the word of God. This description of Sergius Paulus portrays him as a sensitive, secular Gentile leader.

verses.zh: 只是那行法术的以吕马（这名翻出来就是行法术的意思）敌挡使徒，要叫方伯不信真道。
verses.en: But the magician Elymas[NOTE:1] (for that is the way his name is translated)[NOTE:2] opposed them, trying to turn the proconsul[NOTE:3] away from the faith.
notes: On the debate over what the name “Elymas” means, see BDAG 320 s.v. ᾿Ελύμας. The magician’s behavior is more directly opposed to the faith than Simon Magus’ was.
A parenthetical note by the author.
The proconsul was the Roman official who ruled over a province traditionally under the control of the Roman senate.

verses.zh: 扫罗又名保罗，被圣灵充满，定睛看他，
verses.en: But Saul (also known as Paul),[NOTE:1] filled with the Holy Spirit,[NOTE:2] stared straight[NOTE:3] at him
notes: A parenthetical note by the author.
This qualifying clause in the narrative indicates who represented God in the dispute.
Or “gazed intently.”

verses.zh: 说：「你这充满各样诡诈奸恶，魔鬼的儿子，众善的仇敌，你混乱主的正道还不止住吗？
verses.en: and said, “You who are full of all deceit and all wrongdoing,[NOTE:1] you son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness—will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord?[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “unscrupulousness.”

“You who…paths of the Lord?” This rebuke is like ones from the OT prophets: Jer 5:27; Gen 32:11; Prov 10:7; Hos 14:9. Five separate remarks indicate the magician’s failings. The closing rhetorical question of v. 10 (“will you not stop…?”) shows how opposed he is to the way of God.

verses.zh: 现在主的手加在你身上，你要瞎眼，暂且不见日光。」他的眼睛立刻昏蒙黑暗，四下里求人拉着手领他。
verses.en: Now[NOTE:1] look, the hand of the Lord is against[NOTE:2] you, and you will be blind, unable to see the sun for a time!” Immediately mistiness[NOTE:3] and darkness came over[NOTE:4] him, and he went around seeking people[NOTE:5] to lead him by the hand.
notes: Grk “And now.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.
Grk “upon,” but in a negative sense.

The term translated mistiness here appears in the writings of the physician Galen as a medical technical description of a person who is blind. The picture of judgment to darkness is symbolic as well. Whatever power Elymas had, it represented darkness. Magic will again be an issue in Acts 19:18-19. This judgment is like that of Ananias and his wife in Acts 5:1-11.
Grk “fell on.”
The noun χειραγωγός (cheiragōgos) is plural, so “people” is used rather than singular “someone.”

gr.gloss: someone to lead [him] by the hand

verses.zh: 方伯看见所做的事，很希奇主的道，就信了。
verses.en: Then when the proconsul[NOTE:1] saw what had happened, he believed[NOTE:2] because he was greatly astounded[NOTE:3] at the teaching about[NOTE:4] the Lord.
notes: See the note on proconsul in v. 8.
He believed. The faith of the proconsul in the face of Jewish opposition is a theme of the rest of Acts. Paul has indeed become “a light to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:47).
The translation “greatly astounded” for ἐκπλησσόμενος (ekplēssomenos) is given by L&N 25.219.
Grk “of,” but this could give the impression the Lord himself had done the teaching (a subjective genitive) when actually the Lord was the object of the teaching (an objective genitive).

verses.zh: 保罗和他的同人从帕弗开船，来到旁非利亚的别加，约翰就离开他们，回耶路撒冷去。
verses.en: Then Paul and his companions put out to sea[NOTE:1] from Paphos[NOTE:2] and came to Perga[NOTE:3] in Pamphylia,[NOTE:4] but John[NOTE:5] left them and returned to Jerusalem.[NOTE:6]
notes: BDAG 62 s.v. ἀνάγω 4, “as a nautical t.t. (ἀ. τὴν ναῦν put a ship to sea), mid. or pass. ἀνάγεσθαι to begin to go by boat, put out to sea.”
Paphos was a city on the southwestern coast of the island of Cyprus. See Acts 13:6.
Perga was a city in Pamphylia near the southern coast of Asia Minor. The journey from Paphos to Perga is about 105 mi (175 km).
Pamphylia was a province in the southern part of Asia Minor.
That is, John Mark.

Returned to Jerusalem. John Mark had originally accompanied them from Jerusalem (see Acts 12:25). John Mark’s decision to leave became an issue later for Barnabas and Paul (Acts 15:36-39).map For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.

verses.zh: 他们离了别加往前行，来到彼西底的安提阿，在安息日进会堂坐下。
verses.en: Moving on from[NOTE:1] Perga,[NOTE:2] they arrived at Pisidian Antioch,[NOTE:3] and on the Sabbath day they went into[NOTE:4] the synagogue[NOTE:5] and sat down.
notes: Or “Passing by.”
Perga was a city in Pamphylia near the southern coast of Asia Minor.

Or “at Antioch in Pisidia.”sn Pisidian Antioch was a city in Pisidia about 100 mi (160 km) north of Perga. It was both a Roman colony and the seat of military and civil authority in S. Galatia. One had to trek over the Taurus Mountains to get there, since the city was 3,600 ft (1,100 m) above sea level.map For location see JP1-E2; JP2-E2; JP3-E2; JP4-E2.
Grk “going into the synagogue they sat down.” The participle εἰσελθόντες (eiselthontes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.
See the note on synagogue in 6:9.

verses.zh: 读完了律法和先知的书，管会堂的叫人过去，对他们说：「二位兄台，若有甚么劝勉众人的话，请说。」
verses.en: After the reading from the law and the prophets,[NOTE:1] the leaders of the synagogue[NOTE:2] sent them a message,[NOTE:3] saying, “Brothers,[NOTE:4] if you have any message[NOTE:5] of exhortation[NOTE:6] for the people, speak it.”[NOTE:7]
notes: After the reading from the law and the prophets. In the 1st century Jewish synagogue, it was customary after the reading of the Torah (law) and prophets for men to give exhortation from the scriptures.

Normally ἀρχισυνάγωγος (archisunagōgos) refers to the “president of a synagogue” (so BDAG 139 s.v. and L&N 53.93). Since the term is plural here, however, and it would sound strange to the English reader to speak of “the presidents of the synagogue,” the alternative translation “leaders” is used. “Rulers” would also be acceptable, but does not convey quite the same idea.
Grk “sent to them”; the word “message” is an understood direct object. Direct objects in Greek were often omitted when clear from the context, but must be supplied for the modern English reader.
Grk “Men brothers,” but this is both awkward and unnecessary in English.
Or “word.”
Or “encouragement.”
Or “give it.”

verses.zh: 保罗就站起来，举手，说：「以色列人和一切敬畏　神的人，请听。
verses.en: So Paul stood up,[NOTE:1] gestured[NOTE:2] with his hand and said,“Men of Israel,[NOTE:3] and you Gentiles who fear God,[NOTE:4] listen:
notes: This participle, ἀναστάς (anastas), and the following one, κατασείσας (kataseisas), are both translated as adverbial participles of attendant circumstance.
Or “motioned.”

Or “Israelite men,” although this is less natural English. The Greek term here is ἀνήρ (anēr), which only exceptionally is used in a generic sense of both males and females. In this context involving an address to a synagogue gathering, it is conceivable that this is a generic usage, although it can also be argued that Paul’s remarks were addressed primarily to the men present, even if women were there.

Grk “and those who fear God,” but this is practically a technical term for the category called God-fearers, Gentiles who worshiped the God of Israel and in many cases kept the Mosaic law, but did not take the final step of circumcision necessary to become a proselyte to Judaism. See further K. G. Kuhn, TDNT 6:732-34, 743-44.

verses.zh: 这以色列民的　神拣选了我们的祖宗，当民寄居埃及的时候抬举他们，用大能的手领他们出来；
verses.en: The God of this people Israel[NOTE:1] chose our ancestors[NOTE:2] and made the people great[NOTE:3] during their stay as foreigners[NOTE:4] in the country[NOTE:5] of Egypt, and with uplifted arm[NOTE:6] he led them out of it.
notes: Or “people of Israel.”

Or “forefathers”; Grk “fathers.”sn Note how Paul identifies with his audience by referring to our ancestors. He speaks as a Jew. God’s design in history is the theme of the speech. The speech is like Stephen’s, only here the focus is on a promised Son of David.
That is, in both numbers and in power. The implication of greatness in both numbers and in power is found in BDAG 1046 s.v. ὑψόω 2.
Or “as resident aliens.”
Or “land.”
Here uplifted arm is a metaphor for God’s power by which he delivered the Israelites from Egypt. See Exod 6:1, 6; 32:11; Deut 3:24; 4:34; Ps 136:11-12.

verses.zh: 又在旷野容忍（或译：抚养）他们，约有四十年。
verses.en: For[NOTE:1] a period of about forty years he put up with[NOTE:2] them in the wilderness.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “And for.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.
For this verb, see BDAG 1017 s.v. τροποφορέω (cf. also Deut 1:31; Exod 16:35; Num 14:34).
Or “desert.”

verses.zh: 既灭了迦南地七族的人，就把那地分给他们为业；
verses.en: After[NOTE:1] he had destroyed[NOTE:2] seven nations[NOTE:3] in the land of Canaan, he gave his people their land as an inheritance.[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “And after.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.
The participle καθελών (kathelōn) is taken temporally.
Seven nations. See Deut 7:1.
Grk “he gave their land as an inheritance.” The words “his people” are supplied to complete an ellipsis specifying the recipients of the land.

verses.zh: 此后给他们设立士师，约有四百五十年，直到先知撒母耳的时候。
verses.en: All this took[NOTE:1] about 450 years. After this[NOTE:2] he gave them judges until the time of[NOTE:3] Samuel the prophet.
notes: The words “all this took” are not in the Greek text, but are supplied to make a complete statement in English. There is debate over where this period of 450 years fits and what it includes: (1) It could include the years in Egypt, the conquest of Canaan, and the distribution of the land; (2) some connect it with the following period of the judges. This latter approach seems to conflict with 1 Kgs 6:1; see also Josephus, Ant. 8.3.1 (8.61).

Grk “And after these things.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.
The words “the time of” are not in the Greek text, but are implied.

verses.zh: 后来他们求一个王，　神就将便雅悯支派中基士的儿子扫罗，给他们作王四十年。
verses.en: Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul son of Kish, a man from the tribe of Benjamin, who ruled[NOTE:1] forty years.
notes: The words “who ruled” are not in the Greek text, but are implied. They have been supplied as a clarification for the English reader. See Josephus, Ant. 6.14.9 (6.378).

verses.zh: 既废了扫罗，就选立大卫作他们的王，又为他作见证说：『我寻得耶西的儿子大卫，他是合我心意的人，凡事要遵行我的旨意。』
verses.en: After removing him, God[NOTE:1] raised up[NOTE:2] David their king. He testified about him:[NOTE:3] ‘I have found David[NOTE:4] the son of Jesse to be a man after my heart,[NOTE:5] who will accomplish everything I want him to do.’[NOTE:6]
notes: Grk “he”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

The expression raised up refers here to making someone king. There is a wordplay here: “raising up” refers to bringing someone onto the scene of history, but it echoes with the parallel to Jesus’ resurrection.

Grk “about whom.” The relative pronoun (“whom”) was replaced by the pronoun “him” and a new sentence was begun in the translation at this point to improve the English style, due to the length of the sentence in Greek. The verb εἶπεν (eipen) has not been translated (literally “he said testifying”) because it is redundant when combined with the participle μαρτυρήσας (marturēsas, “testifying”). Instead the construction of verb plus participle has been translated as a single English verb (“testified”).
A quotation from Ps 89:20.
A quotation from 1 Sam 13:14.
Or “who will perform all my will,” “who will carry out all my wishes.”

verses.zh: 从这人的后裔中，　神已经照着所应许的，为以色列人立了一位救主，就是耶稣。
verses.en: From the descendants[NOTE:1] of this man[NOTE:2] God brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, just as he promised.[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “From the offspring”; Grk “From the seed.”sn From the descendants (Grk “seed”). On the importance of the seed promise involving Abraham, see Gal 3:6-29.
The phrase this man is in emphatic position in the Greek text.

Grk “according to [his] promise.” The comparative clause “just as he promised” is less awkward in English.sn Just as he promised. Note how Paul describes Israel’s history carefully to David and then leaps forward immediately to Jesus. Paul is expounding the initial realization of Davidic promise as it was delivered in Jesus.

verses.zh: 在他没有出来以先，约翰向以色列众民宣讲悔改的洗礼。
verses.en: Before[NOTE:1] Jesus[NOTE:2] arrived, John[NOTE:3] had proclaimed a baptism for repentance[NOTE:4] to all the people of Israel.
notes: Grk “John having already proclaimed before his coming a baptism…,” a genitive absolute construction which is awkward in English. A new sentence was begun in the translation at this point.
Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the context for clarity, since God is mentioned in the preceding context and John the Baptist in the following clause.
John refers here to John the Baptist.
Grk “a baptism of repentance”; the genitive has been translated as a genitive of purpose.

verses.zh: 约翰将行尽他的程途说：『你们以为我是谁？我不是基督；只是有一位在我以后来的，我解他脚上的鞋带也是不配的。』
verses.en: But while John was completing his mission,[NOTE:1] he said repeatedly,[NOTE:2] ‘What do you think I am? I am not he. But look, one is coming after me. I am not worthy to untie the sandals on his feet!’[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “task.”
The verb ἔλεγεν (elegen) has been translated as an iterative imperfect, since John undoubtedly said this or something similar on numerous occasions.
Literally a relative clause, “of whom I am not worthy to untie the sandals of his feet.” Because of the awkwardness of this construction in English, a new sentence was begun here.

verses.zh: 「弟兄们，亚伯拉罕的子孙和你们中间敬畏　神的人哪，这救世的道是传给我们的。
verses.en: Brothers,[NOTE:1] descendants[NOTE:2] of Abraham’s family,[NOTE:3] and those Gentiles among you who fear God,[NOTE:4] the message[NOTE:5] of this salvation has been sent to us.
notes: Grk “Men brothers,” but this is both awkward and unnecessary in English.
Grk “sons”
Or “race.”

Grk “and those among you who fear God,” but this is practically a technical term for the category called God-fearers, Gentiles who worshiped the God of Israel and in many cases kept the Mosaic law, but did not take the final step of circumcision necessary to become a proselyte to Judaism. See further K. G. Kuhn, TDNT 6:732-34, 743-44. Note how Paul includes God-fearing Gentiles as recipients of this promise.
Grk “word.”

verses.zh: 耶路撒冷居住的人和他们的官长，因为不认识基督，也不明白每安息日所读众先知的书，就把基督定了死罪，正应了先知的预言；
verses.en: For the people who live in Jerusalem and their rulers did not recognize[NOTE:1] him,[NOTE:2] and they fulfilled the sayings[NOTE:3] of the prophets that are read every Sabbath by condemning[NOTE:4] him.[NOTE:5]
notes: BDAG 12-13 s.v. ἀγνοέω 1.b gives “not to know w. acc. of pers.” as the meaning here, but “recognize” is a better translation in this context because recognition of the true identity of the one they condemned is the issue. See Acts 2:22-24; 4:26-28.
Grk “this one.”

Usually φωνή (phōnē) means “voice,” but BDAG 1071-72 s.v. φωνή 2.c has “Also of sayings in scripture…Ac 13:27.” sn They fulfilled the sayings. The people in Jerusalem and the Jewish rulers should have known better because they had the story read to them weekly in the synagogue.
The participle κρίναντες (krinantes) is instrumental here.
The word “him” is not in the Greek text but is implied. Direct objects were often omitted in Greek when clear from the context, but must be supplied for the modern English reader.

verses.zh: 虽然查不出他有当死的罪来，还是求彼拉多杀他；
verses.en: Though[NOTE:1] they found[NOTE:2] no basis[NOTE:3] for a death sentence,[NOTE:4] they asked Pilate to have him executed.
notes: Grk “And though.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.
The participle εὑρόντες (heurontes) has been translated as a concessive adverbial participle.
No basis. Luke insists on Jesus’ innocence again and again in Luke 23:1-25.
Grk “no basis for death,” but in this context a sentence of death is clearly indicated.

verses.zh: 既成就了经上指着他所记的一切话，就把他从木头上取下来，放在坟墓里。
verses.en: When they had accomplished[NOTE:1] everything that was written[NOTE:2] about him, they took him down[NOTE:3] from the cross[NOTE:4] and placed him[NOTE:5] in a tomb.
notes: Or “carried out.”
That is, everything that was written in OT scripture.
Grk “taking him down from the cross, they placed him.” The participle καθελόντες (kathelontes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.
Grk “tree,” but frequently figurative for a cross. The allusion is to Deut 21:23. See Acts 5:30; 10:39.
The word “him” is not in the Greek text but is implied. Direct objects were often omitted in Greek when clear from the context, but must be supplied for the modern English reader.

verses.zh: 神却叫他从死里复活。
verses.en: But God raised[NOTE:1] him from the dead,
notes: See the note on the phrase “raised up” in v. 22, which is the same Greek verb used here.

verses.zh: 那从加利利同他上耶路撒冷的人多日看见他，这些人如今在民间是他的见证。
verses.en: and[NOTE:1] for many days he appeared to those who had accompanied[NOTE:2] him from Galilee to Jerusalem. These[NOTE:3] are now his witnesses to the people.
notes: Grk “who.” The relative pronoun (“who”) was replaced by the conjunction “and” and the pronoun “he” at this point to improve the English style.
Those who had accompanied him refers to the disciples, who knew Jesus in ministry. Luke is aware of resurrection appearances in Galilee though he did not relate any of them in Luke 24.

Grk “who.” The relative pronoun (“who”) was replaced by the demonstrative pronoun “these” and a new sentence was begun in the translation at this point to improve the English style, due to the length of the sentence in Greek and the awkwardness of two relative clauses (“who for many days appeared” and “who are now his witnesses”) following one another.

verses.zh: 我们也报好信息给你们，就是那应许祖宗的话，
verses.en: And we proclaim to you the good news about the promise to our ancestors,[NOTE:1]
notes: Or “to our forefathers”; Grk “the fathers.”

verses.zh: 神已经向我们这作儿女的应验，叫耶稣复活了。正如诗篇第二篇上记着说：你是我的儿子，我今日生你。
verses.en: that this promise[NOTE:1] God has fulfilled to us, their children, by raising[NOTE:2] Jesus, as also it is written in the second psalm, ‘You are my Son;[NOTE:3] today I have fathered you.’[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “that this”; the referent (the promise mentioned in the previous verse) has been specified in the translation for clarity.sn This promise refers to the promise of a Savior through the seed (descendants) of David that is proclaimed as fulfilled (Rom 1:1-7).

Or “by resurrecting.” The participle ἀναστήσας (anastēsas) is taken as instrumental here.sn By raising (i.e., by resurrection) tells how this promise came to be realized, though again the wordplay also points to his presence in history through this event (see the note on “raised up” in v. 22).

You are my Son. The key to how the quotation is used is the naming of Jesus as “Son” to the Father. The language is that of kingship, as Ps 2 indicates. Here is the promise about what the ultimate Davidic heir would be.

A quotation from Ps 2:7.tn Grk “I have begotten you.” The traditional translation for γεγέννηκα (gegennēka, “begotten”) is misleading to the modern English reader because it is no longer in common use. Today one speaks of “fathering” a child in much the same way speakers of English formerly spoke of “begetting a child.”

verses.zh: 论到　神叫他从死里复活，不再归于朽坏，就这样说：我必将所应许大卫那圣洁、可靠的恩典赐给你们。
verses.en: But regarding the fact that he has raised Jesus[NOTE:1] from the dead, never[NOTE:2] again to be[NOTE:3] in a state of decay, God[NOTE:4] has spoken in this way: ‘I will give you[NOTE:5] the holy and trustworthy promises[NOTE:6] made to David.’[NOTE:7]
notes: Grk “him”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Although μηκέτι (mēketi) can mean “no longer” or “no more,” the latter is more appropriate here, since to translate “no longer” in this context could give the reader the impression that Jesus did experience decay before his resurrection. Since the phrase “no more again to be” is somewhat awkward in English, the simpler phrase “never again to be” was used instead.
The translation “to be in again” for ὑποστρέφω (hupostrephō) is given in L&N 13.24.
Grk “he”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The pronoun “you” is plural here. The promises of David are offered to the people.

Or “the trustworthy decrees made by God to David.” The phrase τὰ ὅσια Δαυὶδ τὰ πιστά (ta hosia Dauid ta pista) is “compressed,” that is, in a very compact or condensed form. It could be expanded in several different ways. BDAG 728 s.v. ὅσιος 3 understands it to refer to divine decrees: “I will grant you the sure decrees of God relating to David.” BDAG then states that this quotation from Isa 55:3 is intended to show that the following quotation from Ps 16:10 could not refer to David himself, but must refer to his messianic descendant (Jesus). L&N 33.290 render the phrase “I will give to you the divine promises made to David, promises that can be trusted,” although they also note that τὰ ὅσια in Acts 13:34 can mean “divine decrees” or “decrees made by God.” In contemporary English it is less awkward to translate πιστά as an adjective (“trustworthy”). The concept of “divine decrees,” not very understandable to the modern reader, has been replaced by “promises,” and since God is the implied speaker in the context, it is clear that these promises were made by God.
A quotation from Isa 55:3. The point of this citation is to make clear that the promise of a Davidic line and blessings are made to the people as well.

verses.zh: 又有一篇上说：你必不叫你的圣者见朽坏。
verses.en: Therefore he also says in another psalm,[NOTE:1] ‘You will not permit your Holy One[NOTE:2] to experience[NOTE:3] decay.’[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “Therefore he also says in another”; the word “psalm” is not in the Greek text but is implied.

The Greek word translated “Holy One” here (ὅσιόν, hosion) is related to the use of ὅσια (hosia) in v. 34. The link is a wordplay. The Holy One, who does not die, brings the faithful holy blessings of promise to the people.
Grk “to see,” but the literal translation of the phrase “to see decay” could be misunderstood to mean simply “to look at decay,” while here “see decay” is really figurative for “experience decay.”
A quotation from Ps 16:10.

verses.zh: 「大卫在世的时候遵行了　神的旨意，就睡了（或译：大卫按　神的旨意服事了他那一世的人，就睡了），归到他祖宗那里，已见朽坏；
verses.en: For David, after he had served[NOTE:1] God’s purpose in his own generation, died,[NOTE:2] was buried with his ancestors,[NOTE:3] and experienced[NOTE:4] decay,
notes: The participle ὑπηρετήσας (hupēretēsas) is taken temporally.
The verb κοιμάω (koimaō) literally means “sleep,” but it is often used in the Bible as a euphemism for the death of a believer.
Or “forefathers”; Grk “was gathered to his fathers” (a Semitic idiom).

Grk “saw,” but the literal translation of the phrase “saw decay” could be misunderstood to mean simply “looked at decay,” while here “saw decay” is really figurative for “experienced decay.” This remark explains why David cannot fulfill the promise.

verses.zh: 惟独　神所复活的，他并未见朽坏。
verses.en: but the one[NOTE:1] whom God raised up did not experience[NOTE:2] decay.
notes: The one whom God raised up refers to Jesus.

Grk “see,” but the literal translation of the phrase “did not see decay” could be misunderstood to mean simply “did not look at decay,” while here “did not see decay” is really figurative for “did not experience decay.”

verses.zh: 所以，弟兄们，你们当晓得：赦罪的道是由这人传给你们的。
verses.en: Therefore let it be known to you, brothers, that through this one[NOTE:1] forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you,
notes: That is, Jesus. This pronoun is in emphatic position in the Greek text. Following this phrase in the Greek text is the pronoun ὑμῖν (humin, “to you”), so that the emphasis for the audience is that “through Jesus to you” these promises have come.

verses.zh: 你们靠摩西的律法，在一切不得称义的事上信靠这人，就都得称义了。
verses.en: and by this one[NOTE:1] everyone who believes is justified[NOTE:2] from everything from which the law of Moses could not justify[NOTE:3] you.[NOTE:4]
notes: This one refers here to Jesus.

Or “is freed.” The translation of δικαιωθῆναι (dikaiōthēnai) and δικαιοῦται (dikaioutai) in Acts 13:38-39 is difficult. BDAG 249 s.v. δικαιόω 3 categorizes δικαιωθῆναι in 13:38 (Greek text) under the meaning “make free/pure” but categorizes δικαιοῦται in Acts 13:39 as “be found in the right, be free of charges” (BDAG 249 s.v. δικαιόω 2.b.β). In the interest of consistency both verbs are rendered as “justified” in this translation.
Or “could not free.”

Grk “from everything from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses.” The passive construction has been converted to an active one in the translation, with “by the law of Moses” becoming the subject of the final clause. The words “from everything from which the law of Moses could not justify you” are part of v. 38 in the Greek text, but due to English style and word order must be placed in v. 39 in the translation.

verses.zh: 所以，你们务要小心，免得先知书上所说的临到你们。
verses.en: Watch out,[NOTE:1] then, that what is spoken about by[NOTE:2] the prophets does not happen to you:
notes: The speech closes with a warning, “Watch out,” that also stresses culpability.
Or “in.”

verses.zh: 主说：你们这轻慢的人要观看，要惊奇，要灭亡；因为在你们的时候，我行一件事，虽有人告诉你们，你们总是不信。」
verses.en: ‘Look, you scoffers; be amazed and perish![NOTE:1] For I am doing a work in your days,a work you would never believe, even if someone tells you.’”[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “and die!”

A quotation from Hab 1:5. The irony in the phrase even if someone tells you, of course, is that Paul has now told them. So the call in the warning is to believe or else face the peril of being scoffers whom God will judge. The parallel from Habakkuk is that the nation failed to see how Babylon’s rising to power meant perilous judgment for Israel.

verses.zh: 他们出会堂的时候，众人请他们到下安息日再讲这话给他们听。
verses.en: As Paul and Barnabas[NOTE:1] were going out,[NOTE:2] the people[NOTE:3] were urging[NOTE:4] them to speak about these things[NOTE:5] on the next Sabbath.
notes: Grk “they”; the referents (Paul and Barnabas) have been specified in the translation for clarity.
Or “were leaving.” The participle ἐξιόντων (exiontōn) is taken temporally.
Grk “they”; the referent (the people) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Or “begging,” “inviting.”
Or “matters.”

verses.zh: 散会以后，犹太人和敬虔进犹太教的人多有跟从保罗、巴拿巴的。二人对他们讲道，劝他们务要恒久在　神的恩中。
verses.en: When the meeting of the synagogue[NOTE:1] had broken up,[NOTE:2] many of the Jews and God-fearing proselytes[NOTE:3] followed Paul and Barnabas, who were speaking with them and were persuading[NOTE:4] them[NOTE:5] to continue[NOTE:6] in the grace of God.
notes: See the note on synagogue in 6:9.
BDAG 607 s.v. λύω 3 has “λυθείσης τ. συναγωγῆς when the meeting of the synagogue had broken up Ac 13:43.”

Normally the phrase σεβόμενοι τὸν θεόν (sebomenoi ton theon) refers to Gentiles (“God-fearers”) who believed in God, attended the synagogue, and followed the Mosaic law to some extent, but stopped short of undergoing circumcision. BDAG 918 s.v. σέβω 1.b lists in this category references in Acts 16:14; 18:7; with σεβόμενοι alone, Acts 13:50; 17:4, 17; the phrase is also found in Josephus, Ant. 14.7.2 (14.110). Unique to this particular verse is the combination σεβόμενοι προσηλύτων (sebomenoi prosēlutōn). Later rabbinic discussion suggests that to be regarded as a proper proselyte, a Gentile male had to submit to circumcision. If that is the case here, these Gentiles in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch should be regarded as full proselytes who had converted completely to Judaism and undergone circumcision. It is probably more likely, however, that προσηλύτων is used here in a somewhat looser sense (note the use of σεβομένας [sebomenas] alone to refer to women in Acts 13:50) and that these Gentiles were still in the category commonly called “God-fearers” without being full, technical proselytes to Judaism. See further K. G. Kuhn, TDNT 6:732-34, 743-44. Regardless, the point is that many Gentiles, as well as Jews, came to faith.
This is the meaning given for ἔπειθον (epeithon) in this verse by BDAG 791 s.v. πείθω 1.b.
Grk “who, as they were speaking with them, were persuading them.”
The verb προμένειν (promenein) is similar in force to the use of μένω (menō, “to reside/remain”) in the Gospel and Epistles of John.

verses.zh: 到下安息日，合城的人几乎都来聚集，要听　神的道。
verses.en: On the next Sabbath almost the whole city assembled together to hear the word of the Lord.[NOTE:1]
notes: The word of the Lord is a technical expression in OT literature, often referring to a divine prophetic utterance (e.g., Gen 15:1, Isa 1:10, Jonah 1:1). In the NT it occurs 15 times: 3 times as ῥῆμα τοῦ κυρίου (rhēma tou kuriou; Luke 22:61, Acts 11:16, 1 Pet 1:25) and 12 times as λόγος τοῦ κυρίου (logos tou kuriou; here and in vv. 48 and 49; Acts 8:25; 15:35, 36; 16:32; 19:10, 20; 1 Thess 1:8; 4:15; 2 Thess 3:1). As in the OT, this phrase focuses on the prophetic nature and divine origin of what has been said.tc Most mss (B* C E Ψ M sy bo) read θεοῦ (theou, “of God”) here instead of κυρίου (kuriou, “of the Lord”). Other mss, among them some significant early witnesses (P74 א A B2 33 81 323 945 1175 1739 al sa), read κυρίου. The external evidence favors κυρίου, though not decisively. Internally, the mention of “God” in v. 43, and especially “the word of God” in v. 46, would provide some temptation for scribes to assimilate the wording in v. 44 to these texts.

verses.zh: 但犹太人看见人这样多，就满心嫉妒，硬驳保罗所说的话，并且毁谤。
verses.en: But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy,[NOTE:1] and they began to contradict[NOTE:2] what Paul was saying[NOTE:3] by reviling him.[NOTE:4]
notes: They were filled with jealousy. Their foolish response to the gospel is noted again (see Acts 5:17; 7:9; 17:5).

The imperfect verb ἀντέλεγον (antelegon) has been translated as an ingressive imperfect in the logical sequence of events: After they were filled with jealousy, the Jewish opponents began to contradict what Paul said.
Grk “the things being said by Paul.” For smoothness and simplicity of English style, the passive construction has been converted to active voice in the translation.

The participle βλασφημοῦντες (blasphēmountes) has been regarded as indicating the means of the action of the main verb. It could also be translated as a finite verb (“and reviled him”) in keeping with contemporary English style. The direct object (“him”) is implied rather than expressed and could be impersonal (“it,” referring to what Paul was saying rather than Paul himself), but the verb occurs more often in contexts involving defamation or slander against personal beings (not always God). For a very similar context to this one, compare Acts 18:6. The translation “blaspheme” is not used because in contemporary English its meaning is more narrowly defined and normally refers to blasphemy against God (not what Paul’s opponents were doing here). The modern term “slandering” comes close to what was being done to Paul here.

verses.zh: 保罗和巴拿巴放胆说：「　神的道先讲给你们原是应当的；只因你们弃绝这道，断定自己不配得永生，我们就转向外邦人去。
verses.en: Both Paul and Barnabas replied courageously,[NOTE:1] “It was necessary to speak the word of God[NOTE:2] to you first. Since you reject it and do not consider yourselves worthy[NOTE:3] of eternal life, we[NOTE:4] are turning to the Gentiles.[NOTE:5]
notes: Grk “Both Paul and Barnabas spoke out courageously and said.” The redundancy is removed in the translation and the verb “replied” is used in keeping with the logical sequence of events. The theme of boldness reappears: Acts 4:24-30; 9:27-28.
Grk “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken.” For smoothness and simplicity of English style, the passive construction has been converted to active voice in the translation.
Or “and consider yourselves unworthy.”
Grk “behold, we.” In this context ἰδού (idou) is not easily translated into English.
This turning to the Gentiles would be a shocking rebuke to 1st century Jews who thought they alone were the recipients of the promise.

verses.zh: 因为主曾这样吩咐我们说：我已经立你作外邦人的光，叫你施行救恩，直到地极。」
verses.en: For this[NOTE:1] is what the Lord has commanded us: ‘I have appointed[NOTE:2] you to be a light[NOTE:3] for the Gentiles, to bring salvation[NOTE:4] to the ends of the earth.’”[NOTE:5]
notes: Here οὕτως (houtōs) is taken to refer to what follows, the content of the quotation, as given for this verse by BDAG 742 s.v. οὕτω/οὕτως 2.

BDAG 1004 s.v. τίθημι 3.a has “τιθέναι τινὰ εἴς τι place/appoint someone to or for (to function as) someth….Ac 13:47.” This is a double accusative construction of object (“you”) and complement (“a light”).
Paul alludes here to the language of the Servant in Isaiah, pointing to Isa 42:6; 49:6. He and Barnabas do the work of the Servant in Isaiah.
Grk “that you should be for salvation,” but more simply “to bring salvation.”

An allusion to Isa 42:6 and 49:6. The expression the ends of the earth recalls Luke 3:6 and Acts 1:8. Paul sees himself and Barnabas as carrying out the commission of Luke 24:27. (See 2 Cor 6:2, where servant imagery also appears concerning Paul’s message.)

verses.zh: 外邦人听见这话，就欢喜了，赞美　神的道；凡预定得永生的人都信了。
verses.en: When the Gentiles heard this, they began to rejoice[NOTE:1] and praise[NOTE:2] the word of the Lord, and all who had been appointed for eternal life[NOTE:3] believed.
notes: The imperfect verb ἔχαιρον (echairon) and the following ἐδόξαζον (edoxazon) are translated as ingressive imperfects.

Or “glorify.” Although “honor” is given by BDAG 258 s.v. δοξάζω as a translation, it would be misleading here, because the meaning is “to honor in the sense of attributing worth to something,” while in contemporary English usage one speaks of “honoring” a contract in the sense of keeping its stipulations. It is not a synonym for “obey” in this context (“obey the word of the Lord”), but that is how many English readers would understand it.
Note the contrast to v. 46 in regard to eternal life.

verses.zh: 于是主的道传遍了那一带地方。
verses.en: So the word of the Lord was spreading[NOTE:1] through the entire region.
notes: BDAG 239 s.v. διαφέρω 1 has “spread” for διαφέρετο (diaphereto) in connection with a teaching. This is the first summary since Acts 9:31.

verses.zh: 但犹太人挑唆虔敬、尊贵的妇女和城内有名望的人，逼迫保罗、巴拿巴，将他们赶出境外。
verses.en: But the Jews incited[NOTE:1] the God-fearing women of high social standing and the prominent men of the city, stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and threw them out[NOTE:2] of their region.
notes: For the translation of παρώτρυναν (parōtrunan) as “incited” see BDAG 780 s.v. παροτρύνω.
BDAG 299 s.v. ἐκβάλλω 1 has “throw out.” Once again, many Jews reacted to the message (Acts 5:17, 33; 6:11; 13:45).

verses.zh: 二人对着众人跺下脚上的尘土，就往以哥念去了。
verses.en: So after they shook[NOTE:1] the dust off their feet[NOTE:2] in protest against them, they went to Iconium.[NOTE:3]
notes: The participle ἐκτιναξάμενοι (ektinaxamenoi) is taken temporally. It could also be translated as a participle of attendant circumstance (“So they shook…and went”).
Shaking the dust off their feet was a symbolic gesture commanded by Jesus to his disciples, Matt 10:14; Mark 6:11; Luke 9:5. It shows a group of people as culpable before God.
Iconium was a city in Lycaonia about 90 mi (145 km) east southeast of Pisidian Antioch.

verses.zh: 门徒满心喜乐，又被圣灵充满。
verses.en: And the disciples were filled with joy[NOTE:1] and with the Holy Spirit.
notes: The believers of Pisidian Antioch were not discouraged by the persecution, but instead were filled with joy.

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS TO ACTS 13

- Chapters 13 and 14 are an account of Paul and Barnabas' first missionary journey. The rest of the book of Acts will be given over to Paul's ministry.

- It would be very helpful to turn to the map in the back of your Bible or atlas and follow the geographical locations
mentioned in Acts 13 and 14.

- There is an obvious transition in Acts 13 and 14 from the leadership of Barnabas to the leadership of Paul.

- Notice the series of OT quotes (much like Stephen's sermon)

- v. 33 ‒ Ps. 2:7

- v. 34 ‒ Isa. 55:3

- v. 35 ‒ Ps. 16:10

- v. 41 ‒ Hab. 1:5

- v. 47 ‒ Isa. 49:6

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: ACTS 13:1-3

1Now there were at Antioch, in the church that was there,
prophets and teachers: Barnabas, and Simeon who was called Niger, and Lucius of Cyrene, and Manaen who had been brought
up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. 2While they were ministering to the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, "Set
apart for Me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them." 3Then, when they had fasted and prayed
and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.

13:1 "Antioch" This refers to Antioch of Syria, the third largest city in the Roman Empire. See note at Acts 11:19.

▣ "the church" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: CHURCH (ekklēsia)

▣ "prophets and teachers" These two gifts of the Spirit are listed in 1 Cor. 12:28 and Eph. 4:11.
The grammatical construction is such that it is uncertain whether the five men listed were both prophets
and teachers or if the first three are prophets and the last two are teachers.

The problem with this term is, "How is the NT gift of prophecy related to OT prophets?" In
the OT prophets are writers of Scripture. In the NT this task is given to the original twelve Apostles and
their helpers. As the term "apostle" is retained as an ongoing gift (cf. Eph. 4:11), but with a changed
task after the death of the Twelve, so too, is the office of prophet. Inspiration has ceased; there is no
further inspired Scripture. New Testament prophets' primary task is proclamation of the gospel, but also a
different task, possibly how to apply NT truths to current situations and needs.

The gift of teacher is mentioned in Acts 13:1 in combination with prophecy, but in Eph. 4:11
it is linked with pastors. In 2 Tim. 1:11 Paul says he is a preacher, apostle, and a teacher. Here it
seems to stand independently, as it does in Rom. 12:7. It is also discussed separately in James 3:1ff. This
implies that these leadership gifts can be combined in different ways in different believers to meet the
need of the church in that day or area. Each of these gifted leaders (cf. Eph. 4:11) proclaimed the gospel,
but in different ways (ordering, preaching, instructing).

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (NT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

SPECIAL TOPIC: ILLUMINATION

▣ "Barnabas" See SPECIAL TOPIC: BARNABAS

▣ "Simeon who was called Niger" The term niger is Latin for dark or black. Some commentators
try to relate this Simon to Mark 15:21 who was from Africa and who was forced by the Roman guards to carry Jesus' cross.

▣ "Lucius of Cyrene" Possibly this is one of the Hellenistic Jews that preached to the Gentiles
in Antioch (cf. Acts 11:20). He is probably not the Lucius mentioned in Rom. 16:21.

▣ "Manaen who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch" Manaen is a Greek form of the
Hebrew Manahem, which means "comforter." This man was either a foster brother (Greek literature) of
Herod Antipas (see Introduction to Acts 12) or he grew up with him (Koine papyri). Luke probably got
much of his information about Herod Antipas (the Tetrarch) from conversations with this man.
